findings.title: Findings converge on the uncapped, single-job DEBUG drain
findings.why_it_matters: Five findings land on one mechanism: the budget-exempt DEBUG tier deletes until drained inside one job on the single write queue.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate the uncapped, single-job DEBUG drain before addressing Findings 2-6 individually.
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate the uncapped, single-job DEBUG drain before addressing Findings 2-6 individually.
findings.choice_reason: Wanted as little machinery as possible; re-evaluation settled on no exemption (shared budget), recorded as D3 superseding parent D9's exemption.

findings.title: The uncapped drain holds the single writer long enough to withdraw awaited writes and drop log batches at every level
findings.why_it_matters: Awaited writes withdrawn after 60 s and log batches of every level dropped during a large one-time drain.
findings.recommended: A: Give the DEBUG tier its own per-run bound

findings.title: The startup catch-up runs the uncapped tier inside a shared timeout, starving retention and skipping the shrink
findings.why_it_matters: A large DEBUG backlog consumes the 15 s startup budget, so age retention never runs at startup.

findings.title: The termination guarantee is inferred from queue structure, with no backstop
findings.why_it_matters: A future writer bypassing the queue would make the loop an unbounded writer hold.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation

findings.title: The uncapped job ignores shutdown
findings.why_it_matters: Shutdown during a long drain waits out the drain timeout and may close queued writes unwritten.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation

findings.title: The partial index silently stops being used if the level filter is a bound parameter
A capped DEBUG tier stops the run, so executions go untrimmed while a DEBUG backlog drains, and the docs only cover live capture
findings.why_it_matters: The DEBUG tier is now priority 0. When it uses up the shared budget (`size_failsafe_max_iterations` × `size_failsafe_delete_batch`, 10 × 1,000 by default) and DEBUG rows remain, `capped_early` breaks the priority loop. Framework executions, blocking events and app executions are never reached that cycle. While DEBUG rows keep exceeding about 10k per hour, every table goes untrimmed, so the database can grow past `max_size_mb` without bound, including from executions. DEBUG rows are small, so the ~10k rows deleted per run free little space. D3 accepted this for capture faster than about 2.8 rows/s, "until capture stops". The critics add a case D3's acceptance and the docs leave out: a one-time backlog. An install upgrading from a version where DEBUG lines were exempt can hold far more than 10k of them, and execution trimming then pauses until that backlog drains at 10k rows per hourly run (about 4 days for 1M rows), even with capture off. The new docs paragraph says the database stays over the limit "until the capture stops". In the backlog case that is inaccurate.
findings.recommended: C: Keep D3's behavior. In database-telemetry.md, change "until the capture stops" so it also covers a backlog ("until capture stops and the stored DEBUG lines drain"), and add one sentence: while DEBUG lines above the per-run budget remain, executions aren't trimmed. Add the backlog case to D3's acceptance in the ledger.
findings.chosen: C: Keep D3's behavior. In database-telemetry.md, change "until the capture stops" so it also covers a backlog ("until capture stops and the stored DEBUG lines drain"), and add one sentence: while DEBUG lines above the per-run budget remain, executions aren't trimmed. Add the backlog case to D3's acceptance in the ledger.

findings.title: The capped-tier warning names no setting to change
findings.why_it_matters: The capped state in Finding 1 shows up only as "Size failsafe debug log records capped at 10 iterations; live data still X MB (limit Y MB) — stopping this cycle without touching lower-priority tiers", repeated every hour. D3's recommendation counts on this WARNING plus the user raising `size_failsafe_max_iterations` or `size_failsafe_delete_batch`, but the message names neither setting. The operator has to find them in the docs.
findings.chosen: In `_check_size_failsafe`'s capped warning (src/hassette/core/database_failsafe.py:295-302), add a clause naming the settings, for example: `"... — stopping this cycle without touching lower-priority tiers; raise database.size_failsafe_max_iterations or database.size_failsafe_delete_batch to delete faster"`. This changes message text only and adds no state or branch.

findings.title: Partial-index use relies on SQLite matching a bound `level = ?` to the index predicate
findings.why_it_matters: `row_filter_terms` binds `'DEBUG'` as a parameter. If a user's Python links a SQLite build that doesn't treat a bound `level = ?` as implying `level = 'DEBUG'`, every DEBUG-tier failsafe batch, stale-row probe, empty-tier check and age delete falls back to walking `idx_lr_time`. D2 measured that at about 160-174 ms per statement, and the cost grows with the table. The failure is silent: queries get slower, results stay correct.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: on a SQLite build that doesn't match a bound `level = ?` to the partial-index predicate, DEBUG-tier queries scan `idx_lr_time` (slow, not wrong).
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: on a SQLite build that doesn't match a bound `level = ?` to the partial-index predicate, DEBUG-tier queries scan `idx_lr_time` (slow, not wrong).

findings.title: The age pass's use of the partial index isn't pinned by a test
findings.why_it_matters: `Audience assumption: large log_records tables (millions of rows).` The 022.sql comment says the index serves the age delete and its stale-row probe too, and the Build notes say the EXPLAIN test exists so "a change to the production query shape can't pass unnoticed". That test captures only the failsafe's statements. If the age delete (`... WHERE level = ? AND timestamp < ? LIMIT ?`, no ORDER BY) ever moved to `idx_lr_time`, each hourly age batch would hold the single writer for about 160 ms instead of about 3 ms, and nothing would flag it.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: the age pass's use of `idx_lr_debug_time` is stated in 022.sql but not checked by a test.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: the age pass's use of `idx_lr_debug_time` is stated in 022.sql but not checked by a test.

findings.title: Overlapping log targets report a capped or failed DEBUG age delete under both log labels
findings.why_it_matters: DEBUG rows match both `debug log records` and `log records`. If the DEBUG target hits `retention_max_batches_per_target` in the age pass, `log records` then deletes the rest at the same cutoff and can cap too. The cycle can then log two "hit the N-batch cap" warnings and mark two labels incomplete for overlapping rows. A DELETE failure that hits both (for example a corrupt `idx_lr_debug_time`, which DELETEs on either target maintain) is also reported under both labels. Only the logs are affected. Parent-guard deletes are skipped either way, as they would be with one incomplete label.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: when the DEBUG age delete caps or fails, the cycle may report it under both log labels.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: when the DEBUG age delete caps or fails, the cycle may report it under both log labels.

findings.title: The registry's list position and `priority` both encode the DEBUG-first order
findings.why_it_matters: The failsafe orders tiers by `priority`. The age pass walks `_RETENTION_TABLES` in list order, and the "DEBUG first, so `log records` finds nothing left" behavior comes from list position, tied to `priority` only by a comment. If a later edit reorders the list or inserts a target (such as the near-miss rollups from parent D12), the age-pass order can change silently without any change to `priority`. Correctness doesn't depend on it, since both log targets share a cutoff. The cost is one more delete per age cycle, plus a reader holding two orderings.
findings.recommended: A: Keep list position as the age-pass order, documented by the existing comment.
findings.chosen: B: Make the age pass iterate by `priority`, so one field owns the order.

findings.title: Migration 022 builds its index inside the startup migration timeout on a table that may be large
findings.why_it_matters: `CREATE INDEX ... WHERE level = 'DEBUG'` scans all of `log_records` once, inside `migration_timeout_seconds` (120 s default). The installs that already persisted DEBUG lines have the biggest tables. If the build ran past the timeout, startup would fail for that run. The data-integrity critic confirmed the migration runs inside `BEGIN IMMEDIATE ... COMMIT`, so an interrupted build rolls back cleanly, and the version gate makes it safe to retry.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: the one-time 022 index build runs inside `migration_timeout_seconds` on upgrade.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: the one-time 022 index build runs inside `migration_timeout_seconds` on upgrade.
